hero.title: Molecular Odor Descriptor Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
hero.intro: This project uses a graph neural network to predict, from the structure, the words flavorists would use for its smell, such as fruity, buttery or roasted.

flow.2.title: Graph

flow.4.title: Odor descriptors
flow.4.sub: a probability for each of 138 words
method.data: Data. 4,886 molecules with expert odor descriptions from two flavor and fragrance databases (The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell), merged and cleaned by the OpenPOM project. Each molecule has about 5 of 138 possible descriptors.
method.model: Model. Each atom starts with a few simple properties: element, number of neighbors and hydrogens, charge, aromaticity and whether it is in a ring. Each bond is described by its type (single, double, triple, aromatic) and whether it is in a ring. In each round every atom collects information from the atoms bonded to it, and what it receives depends on both the neighbor and the bond between them, so the same neighbor passes on different information through a single bond than through a double bond. The architecture follows the message passing idea of Lee et al. 2023 (Science 381, 999). The result is pooled into one summary of the whole molecule and turned into 138 probabilities. The model has about 940,000 parameters (a 3.8 MB file) and runs in a web browser.
method.eval: Data split. Molecules with rings were split into training (80%), validation (10%) and test (10%) sets by ring scaffold, so the test set contains ring systems the model never saw. This is harder than a random split.
method.explain: Atom contributions. The coloring on the tool page uses occlusion: each atom is removed in turn (together with its bonds), the model is run again, and the change in the descriptor's probability is recorded. Atoms whose removal lowers the probability (orange) are what the model relies on; atoms whose removal raises it (blue) hold the prediction down. This shows which structures the model weighs, not that they chemically determine the odor.
results.intro: Performance is measured with AUROC. Take one molecule that has a descriptor and one that does not: AUROC is the chance that the model gives the first one a higher score. 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect. The numbers below are averaged over all 138 descriptors on the 488 test molecules.
results.seed_note: Graph neural network: scores of the model deployed on this page. Across 3 training runs with different random seeds, the overall score was {mean} (standard deviation {std}). The baselines describe each molecule by a list of the small structural fragments it contains (a Morgan fingerprint) and use standard machine learning methods.
results.takeaway: The graph neural network beats both conventional baselines by about 0.03 AUROC. The gain is modest but consistent across random seeds and across most descriptors. Molecules with ring systems not seen during training are clearly harder (about 0.81).
results.label_note: Only descriptors with at least 10 positive molecules in the test set are listed.
ablation.intro: Two ideas from PharmaGNN (Liu et al., J Sci Food Agric 106, 8114-8120, 2026, doi:10.1002/jsfa.70826) were tested: an asymmetric loss (ASL) that puts more weight on rare descriptors, and three pharmacophore flags per atom (hydrogen-bond donor, hydrogen-bond acceptor, hydrophobic group; RDKit's standard definitions, which the browser can reproduce exactly). The paper's 3D charge and logP descriptors cannot be computed identically in the browser and were not used. Each of the four setups was trained 3 times on the same scaffold split:
ablation.cfg.A: Previous model (used on this page at the time)
ablation.note: Test AUROC: mean ± standard deviation over 3 training runs. Rare descriptors: mean AUROC over the third of descriptors with the fewest positive training molecules ({n}). These experiments were run on the previous model (a graph convolutional network that ignores bond types); the model now used on this page is described in 3.4.
ablation.takeaway: The differences between the four setups are within run-to-run noise, and rare descriptors got slightly worse, so this page kept the original model at the time. Possible reasons: the paper used a random split, while this site uses a harder scaffold split; the pharmacophore flags overlap with the existing element and hydrogen-count features; and the paper's model architecture differs. The asymmetric loss also inflates output probabilities about fourfold, which is unsuitable for display.
limits.4: Predictions for ring systems unlike anything in the training data are noticeably weaker (AUROC about 0.81).
limits.6: Not for safety decisions. The model says nothing about toxicity, allergenicity or regulatory status; the EU, China and US status shown separately on the page comes from the official lists and is for reference only.
footer.data: Data and acknowledgements: the model was trained on data from The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell & Associates (Sanchez-Lengeling et al., 2019, arXiv:1910.10685, CC BY-NC), curated and merged by OpenPOM (Barsainyan et al., 2023); the raw data and odor labels are not redistributed here. The model and its predictions are for non-commercial academic demonstration only.
footer.thr: Odor thresholds: L.J. van Gemert, Odour Thresholds: Compilations of Odour Threshold Values in Air, Water and Other Media, 2nd ed., Oliemans Punter & Partners, 2011. Representative values are taken where available from Czerny et al., Eur. Food Res. Technol. 228, 265-273 (2008), as listed there.
footer.ref: Related work: Lee et al., A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception, Science 381, 999-1006 (2023). doi:10.1126/science.ade4401; Liu et al., PharmaGNN: a model for odor prediction based on graph neural networks, J Sci Food Agric 106, 8114-8120 (2026). doi:10.1002/jsfa.70826
footer.fi: Used in: Dairy Flavor Improver (as the single-molecule odor source).

hero.sub: Enter a molecule; a graph neural network predicts its odor descriptors.
footer.short: Trained on The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell data curated by OpenPOM (CC BY-NC). Non-commercial academic demo only; not for safety decisions. See method & sources.
about.practice: For an unfamiliar compound, I usually check odor databases or search the literature with the compound name. Predicting odor from structure can be a useful reference when the molecule closely resembles known compounds, belongs to a homologous series with clear odor trends, and is backed by reliable experimental data. It is less reliable for isomers, especially stereoisomers. The model on this site does not distinguish stereoisomers, so its predictions for these molecules are only a rough hint.
results.compare.title: Comparison with the previous model
results.compare.intro: This page previously used a graph convolutional network that ignores bond types and only sees which atoms are bonded. All three models use the same data split and training settings and were each trained with 3 random seeds; the new model's settings (number of layers, size, update rule) were chosen on the validation set only, and the test set was evaluated once at the end. The table shows the test AUROC averaged over the 138 descriptors (mean ± standard deviation over 3 training runs):
results.compare.gcn: Previous: graph convolutional network (no bond types)
results.compare.mpnn: This page: message passing network (with bond features)
results.compare.nobond: Control: the same message passing network without bond features
results.compare.takeaway: Test macro-averaged AUROC rose from 0.860 to 0.866 (mean of 3 seeds). In the control experiment without bond features it was 0.863, so about half of the gain comes from the bond features, and more clearly so for molecules with rings.

proc.sub: Follow the graph neural network step by step as it turns a molecular structure into odor descriptors. Every number on screen is a real value computed by the model.
proc.say.input_a: Each atom is described by 6 properties (encoded as 26 numbers): element, number of bonded heavy atoms, number of hydrogens, charge, aromatic or not, in a ring or not.
proc.say.input_b: Each bond is described by its type (single, double, triple, aromatic or other) and whether it is in a ring (encoded as 6 numbers). The bond color shows its type.
proc.say.embed_a: One linear transformation turns the 26 numbers of every atom into 256 numbers, one colored strip per atom.
proc.say.embed_b: At this point each atom knows only itself: atoms of the same kind have identical strips.
proc.say.layer_a: Each atom receives messages from the atoms bonded to it. A message depends on the neighbor's current values and on the type of the bond; the color of a moving dot shows the bond type.
proc.say.layer_b: The messages are added up, and the atom adds a new part to its values; existing values never decrease. Cells that light up are what this layer adds.
proc.say.layer_c: After layer {t}, each atom depends only on atoms within {b}. Light green marks this range for the selected atom.
proc.say.pool_a: The results of all atoms are combined into 512 numbers for the whole molecule: 256 are the mean over the atoms, 256 the maximum.
proc.say.out_a: Two fully connected layers turn these 512 numbers into probabilities for 138 descriptors; the top 8 are shown, as on the tool page.
proc.strips_h0: 256 numbers per atom (after the input embedding)
proc.hint_rows: One row per atom; click a row to select that atom.
proc.hint_fine: Many atoms, so the strips are drawn as a fine heat map: one row per atom; click a row to see that atom's strips enlarged.
proc.layer_title: Selected atom: {a} (after layer {t} it depends on {k} atoms)
proc.row_cur: Result of this layer (after layer {t}) = previous + added
proc.detail_hint: Click an atom or a bond in the structure, or a strip, to look at another atom.
proc.bondterms_intro: A message is ReLU(linear transformation of the neighbor's values + bond term). The bond term depends only on the bond class; below are the bond terms of this layer (model weights, before the ReLU, positive or negative): teal is positive, orange negative. The same neighbor sends a different message through a different type of bond.
proc.note_colour: Color shows only the size of a value: darker is larger, 0 is the lightest. The four atom layers share one scale (darkest at the 99th percentile of layer 3 values on the training set, square-root mapping), because the residual update only makes values larger; values above it are drawn darkest. Message sums, mean and maximum each have their own scale.
proc.note_order: The 256 columns are ordered by how the values correlate on the training set, so correlated columns sit together; all four layers use the same order. This is only a way of drawing; a single cell has no chemical meaning of its own.
proc.note_real: All numbers are real model results (4 decimals). The example molecules are computed in advance, so this page loads no model.
proc.note_more: The model structure, the receptive field experiment and the training are described under Methods and sources.
proc.pool_note: Mean and maximum each have their own color scale, so the two strips show similar patterns: columns that are large in the atoms tend to be large in both. The difference is in size: summed over the 256 numbers, the mean of {name} is {p}% of the maximum. The more atoms there are and the more they differ, the lower this share: {cmp}.
proc.pool_cmp_both: for example 57% for diacetyl and 22% for vanillin

pa.intro: The How it predicts page shows, step by step and with the values the model actually computes, how a molecular structure becomes odor descriptors. Below: which part of the model each step corresponds to, and how the page draws it.
pa.s1: Input. Each atom is described by 6 properties encoded as 26 numbers: element (C, N, O, S, F, Cl, Br, I, P or other, 10 classes), number of bonded heavy atoms (0 to 5, more counted as 5), number of hydrogens (0 to 4), charge (−1, 0, +1), aromatic or not, in a ring or not. Each bond is described by its type (single, double, triple, aromatic or other) and whether it is in a ring, encoded as 6 numbers.
pa.s2: Input embedding. One linear transformation (followed by ReLU) turns the 26 numbers of every atom into 256 numbers. At this point each atom reflects only its own properties; atoms with the same properties have identical values.
pa.s3: Message passing (3 layers). In layer t, the message from atom j to a bonded atom i is ReLU(Ut hj + Vt eij + bt), where hj are the current 256 numbers of j and eij the 6 numbers of the bond. A message therefore depends on both the neighbor and the bond type: the term Vt eij + bt depends only on the bond class, and it is what the page shows under "What the bond type adds". Each atom adds up the messages it receives and then makes a residual update: hi gains ReLU(Wt [hi, sum of messages] + ct). The added part is never below 0, so every value can only grow from layer to layer, and a column is the same channel in every layer. Each of the three layers has its own parameters.
pa.s4: Pooling. The mean and the maximum over all atoms of the molecule, 256 numbers each, give 512 numbers for the whole molecule.
pa.s5: Output. Two fully connected layers (512 to 512 with ReLU, then to 138) and a sigmoid give one probability for each of the 138 descriptors. The page shows the top 8, as the tool page does; the 512 numbers between the two layers are not drawn.
pa.field: Receptive field. After layer t, the result of an atom depends only on atoms within t bonds and on the bonds between them; after 3 layers it reaches at most 3 bonds away, and structure further apart comes together only in the pooling step. This was checked on the model: when the carbon at the end of decane is replaced by nitrogen, layers 1, 2 and 3 change only the atoms within 1, 2 and 3 bonds of it, and the other atoms differ by exactly 0; when only one single bond in the middle of the chain is made double, with the atom properties unchanged, layer 1 changes only the 2 atoms of that bond, layer 2 one bond further on each side, layer 3 two bonds further. The check is repeated every time the page data are generated.
pa.display: How the values are drawn. Color shows only the size of a value, with a square-root mapping. The four atom layers share one scale whose darkest color is the 99th percentile of all layer 3 values on the training set (3,910 molecules, 47,944 atoms), 3.278, because the residual update only makes values larger; message sums, mean and maximum each use their own 99th percentile (2.036, 1.940, 6.008); the bond terms can be positive or negative and use two colors. The 256 columns are ordered by average-linkage clustering on the correlation distance (1 − r) of layer 3 values over training atoms, with optimal leaf ordering, so correlated columns sit together; all four layers use the same order. This changes no value; a single cell has no chemical meaning of its own.
pa.values: Where the values come from. The example molecules (the 10 presets of the tool page and methanethiol) are computed in advance with the same model file, to 4 decimals, so the page loads no model for them. Other molecules come from "See how it predicts" below a result on the tool page: the tool page stores only the model inputs (atom and bond encodings, 2D coordinates, SMILES) in the browser's session storage, and the How it predicts page computes every layer in the browser with the same model file as the tool page. The model file also outputs the intermediate results; the tool page reads only the final probabilities, and its predictions are bit for bit the same as with the previous file. Browser and Python agree layer by layer on 50 test molecules (largest relative difference 3e-6), and the 8 descriptors and probabilities on the How it predicts page equal those on the tool page.
